guides.title: What ruqyah is, and where it begins
guides.summary: Healing, reliance on Allah and the conditions for permissible recitation.

sections.title: Healing is sought from Allah
sections.text: Ruqyah uses recitation and supplication to seek Allah’s help. Quran 17:82 describes healing and mercy; 26:80 attributes healing to Allah. A recording, reader or object has no independent power.

sections.title: The central boundary
sections.text: Muslim 2200 permits ruqyah free from shirk. Recognised scholarly guidance stresses intelligible, sound wording and belief that Allah grants healing. Secret invocations whose meaning cannot be explained do not provide that transparency.

label.en: Darul Iftaa Chicago: conditions of ruqyah

sections.title: Three labels in this library
sections.text: A reported practice follows a particular narration. A guided selection combines sourced readings for convenience. Scholarly guidance explains interpretation and practical questions. These labels describe the evidence, not a person’s spiritual rank.

sections.title: The themes behind the words
sections.text: Understanding the passages helps distinguish an appeal to Allah from treating sound or a number as an independent mechanism. The selected readings have different emphases; they are not interchangeable claims about one particular illness.
points: Al-Fatihah brings praise, worship, reliance and a request for guidance together. Its use as ruqyah is also explicitly recognised in the companion’s encounter recorded in Bukhari 5736.
Al-Ikhlas affirms Allah’s oneness and self-sufficiency. Al-Falaq asks for refuge from created harms, darkness, harmful magic and envy; An-Nas asks refuge from whispering.
Ayat al-Kursi describes Allah’s life, knowledge, authority and preservation. Read its complete wording rather than reducing it to a protective symbol.

guides.body: Healing, reliance on Allah and the conditions for permissible recitation.

label.en: Darul Iftaa Chicago: conditions of ruqyah

guides.title: A complete approach to self-ruqyah
guides.summary: Prepare, understand the readings and follow each practice in its own context.

sections.title: Begin with a clear intention
sections.text: Choose a comfortable place and ask Allah for help. Read the meaning before starting if useful. This guide adds no initiation, special clothing, purchased product or compulsory daily course.

sections.title: Read the actual passages
sections.text: Al-Fatihah has an explicit ruqyah report. Al-Falaq and An-Nas occur in the illness practice. Read their complete displayed text carefully; the app’s convenient combined order is not itself a quoted Prophetic sequence.

sections.title: Understand the physical actions
sections.text: The illness report describes gentle blowing and wiping. It does not make forceful spitting, pain or dramatic reactions part of the method. Use the distinct bedtime guide for its specified three-cycle routine.

sections.title: Continue normal care
sections.text: Pause when tired or uncomfortable, and continue appropriate treatment. Progress saved by the app means reading progress; it is not a medical result or proof of a hidden diagnosis.

sections.title: Choose a method that matches the situation
sections.text: Use the purpose of each report to choose where to start. You do not need to complete every routine in this library in one sitting. This is a practical navigation suggestion, not an additional religious obligation.
points: For a painful place in your own body, open the bodily-pain method: the two stages and hand-placement instruction belong together.
For the three-surah bedtime practice, open Bedtime rather than assuming the illness reading and bedtime cycle are identical.
When visiting someone ill, choose the visiting method and notice the wording addressed to another person.
For a general self-reading, the short guided selection brings together separately sourced passages. Read its explanation before treating its order as prescribed.

guides.body: Prepare, understand the readings and follow each practice in its own context.

guides.title: Bodily pain: the three-then-seven method
guides.summary: Hand placement, separate counts and the meaning of seeking refuge.

sections.title: The reported setting
sections.text: Uthman ibn Abi al-As described pain in his body. The Prophet ﷺ taught a hand placement and a two-part supplication. The instruction concerns the pain he reported; it does not identify its medical cause.

sections.title: Follow the two stages
sections.text: Place your hand on the painful area. Say Bismillah three times. Then say the refuge supplication seven times. Complete one stage before moving to the next; each has its own counter.

sections.title: Keep the scope clear
sections.text: The supplication names felt pain and feared harm. It does not promise a recovery deadline. Read with hope while obtaining care for severe, new or persistent pain.

sections.title: Understand what you are asking
sections.text: The first stage begins in Allah’s name. The second seeks refuge in Allah and His power from the harm presently felt and the harm feared. It gives the sufferer words to speak directly; another person’s touch or an audio track is not a substitute specified by this report. The app preserves this narration’s wording rather than silently combining it with similar invocations.

guides.body: Hand placement, separate counts and the meaning of seeking refuge.

guides.title: Bedtime: what completes one cycle?
guides.summary: Three surahs, gentle blowing, wiping and three complete cycles.

sections.title: The complete practice
sections.text: Bring your hands together, recite Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas, gently blow over the hands and wipe the body. Begin with the head, face and front of the body, covering what you can.

sections.title: Count whole cycles
sections.text: The report describes doing the whole practice three times. This reader therefore repeats all three surahs and the wiping step together. Repeating only the final surah is not how its cycle counter is arranged.

sections.title: Other night readings are separate
sections.text: Ayat al-Kursi and Al-Baqarah’s final two verses have their own night reports. Read the complete passages. Their inclusion in the separate night selection does not make them steps of this three-surah cycle.

sections.title: A practical reading checklist
sections.text: The physical action is part of the reported practice, while the on-screen navigation simply helps you follow it. Each completed cycle returns to the first surah; the app does not count a recording as your own recitation.
points: Keep the hands together and use gentle blowing as described in the report, without forceful expulsion of saliva.
Read all three complete surahs. Their displayed order is Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas.
Wipe what you can of the body, beginning with the head, face and front. Then repeat the complete practice until three cycles are finished.

guides.body: Three surahs, gentle blowing, wiping and three complete cycles.

guides.title: Morning, evening and stopping at a place
guides.summary: Match each remembrance to its timing and its own source.

sections.title: The three short surahs
sections.text: Abu Dawud 5082 teaches Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas three times in the morning and evening. It is graded Hasan by Al-Albani on the linked source. The bedtime blowing/wiping method is a separate report.

sections.title: The invocation against sudden affliction
sections.text: Abu Dawud 5088 specifies three recitations in the morning or evening and the following evening or morning as the report’s time span. It should not be expanded into immunity from every illness or life trial.

sections.title: The perfect-words supplication
sections.text: Muslim 2708a gives a stopping-place context; 2708b/2709a also records an evening context. The Muslim reports cited here give no numerical count, so this reader assigns none.

sections.title: Keep the settings distinct
sections.text: Morning/evening remembrance and stopping at a place have different settings. The morning and evening lists combine separate reports for convenient reading; the combined list is not presented as one hadith. An unfamiliar location does not require you to wait for evening before using the stopping-place supplication. Follow each source’s setting rather than assigning one timetable to everything.

guides.body: Match each remembrance to its timing and its own source.

guides.title: Reciting for someone who is ill
guides.summary: Reported wording, the sevenfold visiting dua and the person’s comfort.

sections.title: Know whom the words address
sections.text: Bismillahi arqika addresses another person. The displayed “ishfihi” wording asks Allah to heal him. These forms are preserved as narrated; a grammatical change should be understood rather than mistaken for the exact source wording.

sections.title: The sevenfold visiting supplication
sections.text: Abu Dawud 3106 teaches seven recitations and includes the condition that the person’s appointed time has not arrived. We cannot know that condition or use an outcome to blame the patient.

sections.title: Care and boundaries
sections.text: Explain what you will recite and respect consent, privacy and religious boundaries. The app combines separate reports for convenience; it does not present its combined order as a single transmitted ritual.

sections.title: A bedside visit is more than a counter
sections.text: Read in a way the person can comfortably receive. The app’s visiting method begins with a reminder to explain what you will say. Its sevenfold supplication is addressed to the patient, while other healing wordings have their own grammatical form and context. Finishing the steps records your reading; it does not reveal the person’s appointed time or predict the course of their illness.

guides.body: Reported wording, the sevenfold visiting dua and the person’s comfort.

guides.title: Protection for children, with gentleness
guides.summary: The reported refuge wording and practical care for a child.

sections.title: The report and its wording
sections.text: Bukhari 3371 reports the Prophet ﷺ seeking protection for Al-Hasan and Al-Husayn and recalling Ibrahim’s protection for Ismail and Ishaq. The displayed version keeps the general refuge wording of that report.

sections.title: Comfort is part of care
sections.text: Recite calmly and stop if the child is distressed. Do not frighten, restrain, hurt or interrogate a child to produce a reaction. A caregiver’s concern should also lead to appropriate assessment when a child is unwell.

sections.title: Counts and ordinary precautions
sections.text: This cited report gives no fixed count. The supplication names harmful creatures and harmful eyes, while ordinary safety, hygiene and healthcare remain necessary parts of looking after a child.

guides.body: The reported refuge wording and practical care for a child.

guides.title: Disturbing dreams and whispering
guides.summary: Two reported situations, two methods, without diagnosing hidden causes.

sections.title: After an unpleasant dream
sections.text: Muslim 2262 instructs light spitting to the left three times, seeking Allah’s refuge from Shaytan three times, and turning to the other sleeping side. The guided reading separates the actions so their counts remain clear.

sections.title: Whispering during prayer
sections.text: Muslim 2203a addresses Uthman ibn Abi al-As’s disrupted prayer and recitation. Seeking refuge and the reported three light spits to the left belong to that account. Avoid soiling people or a place of prayer.

sections.title: A response is not a diagnosis
sections.text: A dream, yawn or intrusive thought does not identify who harmed you or prove possession. Persistent distress deserves supportive help; this app offers recitation guidance and does not test a person for unseen causes.

guides.body: Two reported situations, two methods, without diagnosing hidden causes.

guides.title: Evidence, repetition and reading order
guides.summary: How to read the counters and distinguish a method from an app arrangement.

sections.title: One count does not fit every reading
sections.text: The evidence specifies three then seven for bodily pain, three complete cycles for bedtime, and three recitations for the morning/evening short surahs. Their contexts and units differ.

sections.title: What an unspecified count means
sections.text: Where the cited source gives no number, the app provides Read/Next rather than inventing a prescribed count. A personal habit or convenient order should be identified as such, not attributed to the Prophet ﷺ without evidence.

sections.title: Reading progress has a limited meaning
sections.text: Counters record the actions you mark yourself. Listening does not tick them. Completion indicates that reading steps were marked, not that an illness has ended or that a person has reached a spiritual level.

sections.title: How to read a source in this library
sections.text: Open Sources & context and inspect the collection, reference and the practice it actually describes. A source that supports the Arabic wording does not automatically support every number, physical action or benefit attached to it elsewhere. The displayed Hasan/Sahih labels for Sunan reports name the scholar used by the linked edition; they are not a claim that no scholar ever discussed the grading. Quranic selections and scholarly interpretations are labelled separately.

guides.body: How to read the counters and distinguish a method from an app arrangement.

guides.title: Al-Baqarah, the home and selected verses
guides.summary: Full-surah reports, night passages and additional verse selections.

sections.title: The full-surah report
sections.text: Muslim 780 describes Shaytan fleeing a home where Al-Baqarah is recited. That report concerns the surah; the app does not turn a short excerpt into the complete-surah reading.

sections.title: Two night practices
sections.text: Ayat al-Kursi and the final two verses have separate bedtime/night reports. They can be read from the complete passages here without downloading the whole Quran, but each source’s wording and timing remain its own.

sections.title: Verses about Musa and magic
sections.text: Quran 7:117–122, 10:81–82 and 20:69 recount Musa’s encounter with the magicians. Including such passages in a reading selection is different from proving one fixed Prophetic ruqyah list, count or compulsory order.

sections.title: The supplications of Ayyub and Yunus
sections.text: The full verses are included so that familiar dua phrases remain connected to their setting. Ayyub acknowledges suffering and Allah’s mercy; the following verse describes Allah answering him. Yunus’s call combines Allah’s oneness, glorification and acknowledgement of wrongdoing; 21:88 describes rescue from distress. These accounts support hope and humility. Their inclusion here does not assign a new fixed ruqyah count.

guides.body: Full-surah reports, night passages and additional verse selections.

guides.title: Evil eye, sihr and careful conclusions
guides.summary: Respect the religious texts without turning symptoms into an app diagnosis.

sections.title: What the texts affirm
sections.text: Muslim 2188 affirms the evil eye within Islamic teaching. Al-Falaq seeks refuge from envy and other harms. These texts are a basis for prayer and refuge, not permission to accuse a particular relative, neighbour or practitioner.

sections.title: What this app cannot establish
sections.text: No checklist of dreams, headaches, yawning, crying or reactions to an audio track can establish an unseen cause here. Personal experiences deserve care and a fair assessment rather than a certainty the app cannot justify.

sections.title: Seek refuge without escalating fear
sections.text: Use the supported readings calmly, maintain ordinary relationships and seek qualified religious or clinical help when needed. A practitioner’s dramatic claim or a temporary reaction does not replace sound evidence.

sections.title: What to understand about sihr
sections.text: Quran 2:102 condemns learning harmful magic and states that harm is not independent of Allah’s permission. Al-Falaq includes seeking refuge from harmful magical practices and envy. The response presented here is to turn to Allah with supported words. These texts do not supply this app with a way to identify a perpetrator, decode a dream or determine why a particular marriage, illness or setback occurred.

guides.body: Respect the religious texts without turning symptoms into an app diagnosis.

guides.title: Water, oil and commercial ruqyah products
guides.summary: Distinguish scholarly permission from a required Prophetic recipe.

sections.title: The scholarly discussion
sections.text: Jordan’s Iftaa Department permits recitation and blowing over water or oil in its guidance. That is presented here as scholarly guidance; it does not establish a single required ingredient, brand or universal treatment schedule.

sections.title: A product is not a prerequisite
sections.text: The core self-reading methods are available without buying a ruqyah product. Mufti Wilayah discusses safeguards against commercial misuse of Quranic verses. Avoid guaranteed-cure marketing or claims that one seller controls access to healing.

label.en: Mufti Wilayah 829: Quranic writing and commercial misuse
label.bn: মুফতি উইলায়াহ ৮২৯: কুরআনের লেখা ও বাণিজ্যিক অপব্যবহার

sections.title: Health and consent still apply
sections.text: Use only what is safe and suitable for the person. This app gives no ink, chemical, burning or ingestion recipe. Do not compel someone to drink or use a substance; ask qualified help about religious details and medical suitability.

guides.body: Distinguish scholarly permission from a required Prophetic recipe.

guides.title: Purity, menstruation and recitation
guides.summary: Separate dua and remembrance from rulings about tilawah and a physical Mushaf.

sections.title: Different acts have different rulings
sections.text: Making dua, remembering Allah, reciting Quran and handling a physical Mushaf are distinct questions. Do not assume that one short rule answers every situation involving a ruqyah reader.

sections.title: Recognise scholarly differences
sections.text: Egypt’s Dar Al-Ifta records the majority restriction on Quran recitation during menstruation and the Maliki allowance. Jordan’s guidance distinguishes words used as dua or dhikr from recitation intended as tilawah. These are attributed positions, not one universal ruling issued by the app.

sections.title: Get guidance for your circumstances
sections.text: Follow a qualified scholar familiar with your school and circumstances for questions about intention, major impurity and a physical Mushaf. The app keeps meanings and learning material accessible and does not infer your state of purity.

label.en: Darul Iftaa Chicago: conditions of ruqyah

guides.body: Separate dua and remembrance from rulings about tilawah and a physical Mushaf.

label.en: Darul Iftaa Chicago: conditions of ruqyah

guides.title: If recovery takes time
guides.summary: Hope, patience and appropriate treatment without blaming the person who is ill.

sections.title: Illness is not a spiritual score
sections.text: Quran 2:155–157 speaks of trials and patience. Bukhari 5641–5642 describes hardship and illness as occasions for expiation. A slow recovery does not give this app grounds to judge someone’s faith or worth.

sections.title: Care can happen alongside recitation
sections.text: Continue prescribed treatment and seek assessment for ongoing physical or psychological distress. Ruqyah can accompany care; a reading counter is not a test of diagnosis, treatment success or the need for medicine.

sections.title: Act on immediate danger
sections.text: Severe breathing difficulty, unconsciousness, serious injury or another immediate danger calls for urgent local medical help. Pause the session and prioritise getting help; the app does not determine an emergency’s cause.

guides.body: Hope, patience and appropriate treatment without blaming the person who is ill.

guides.title: Choosing trustworthy help
guides.summary: Transparent recitation, clear boundaries and protection from exploitation.

sections.title: Ask what will be read
sections.text: Choose someone who can explain the words and their sources and who respects religious boundaries. MUIS warns against dubious invocations, impure materials and inappropriate seclusion or touching in the name of spiritual healing.

sections.title: Agree clear terms
sections.text: The Al-Fatihah report includes compensation, so a fee alone is not the test of authenticity. Seek transparent terms and avoid pressure, guaranteed outcomes or claims that your family must depend exclusively on one person.

sections.title: Keep control of your care
sections.text: You may stop a session, bring a trusted companion and seek another opinion. Force, injury, sexual contact, isolation from support or a demand to abandon needed medical care are not accepted practices in this app’s guidance.

guides.body: Transparent recitation, clear boundaries and protection from exploitation.

guides.title: Listening, pronunciation and source notes
guides.summary: Use the audio as a learning aid and understand what each source label means.

sections.title: Read with understanding
sections.text: Pronunciation in English or Bangla helps a learner but cannot represent every Arabic sound precisely. Listen, practise gently and learn from a competent teacher where possible. The Arabic text remains the wording reference.

sections.title: Recordings and personal recitation
sections.text: Quran audio is Mishary Rashid Alafasy’s recitation from Al Quran Cloud. Play/download fetches only the selected passage. Listening does not mark your own recitation count or establish that every reported physical action was performed.

sections.title: Credit, availability and reuse
sections.text: Meanings here are app-prepared renderings. Recitations remain the reciter’s copyright; provider terms permit personal/educational streaming and download, with commercial rights retained. Checked matching supplication recordings will be added when available; no synthetic voice replaces them.

guides.body: Use the audio as a learning aid and understand what each source label means.
